source.title: Superposition disentanglement of neural representations reveals hidden alignment
source.authors: André Longon; D. Klindt; Meenakshi Khosla

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether superposition affects representational alignment and whether SAEs improve alignment. It does not test the audit shares, neuron explanations on held-out activations, explanation scores, attribution graphs, or the other specific claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported alignment outcomes concern a related question, not any listed version. They are recorded with versions ["none"] and summarized under fits_no_version. Values available only in figures are marked accordingly. The paper also cites prior work, which is not counted as a result here.
record.test_reason: The paper takes the superposition hypothesis as its premise. It tests whether SAE disentanglement raises cross-model and model-to-brain alignment scores. It never measures what share of neurons have one main job. It does not test explanation accuracy on held-out activations, automated explanation scores or attribution graphs. It also does not re-examine the cat-and-car neuron. Its results bear on representational alignment, a different construct from any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that differing superposition arrangements deflate predictive-mapping alignment and that disentanglement is needed to reveal true alignment. They caveat that SAE artifacts or newly constructed representations might drive the increases, and that SAE→SAE regression underperforms Neuron→Neuron in most settings.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains TopK sparse autoencoders on toy and ImageNet-trained visual-network activations and compares alignment metrics; it does not use the original audit or explanation-testing procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The soft-matching result varies by architecture and layer: ResNet50 decreases at its intermediate layer and increases at its deep layer; ViT-B/16 increases at both, with larger gains at depth. Linear regression results depend on whether one or both representations are SAE-transformed.

fits_no_version.finding: Differently seeded toy models represent shared features in different superposition arrangements: almost all neurons have a max semi-matching correlation below 0.5. SAE latents raise soft-matching alignment for N=16 and N=32 but lower it for N=8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, the same features can be superposed differently across seeds, which deflates neuron-level alignment metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: In ImageNet models, SAE latents lower soft-matching alignment at the ResNet50 intermediate layer and raise it at deep layers. ViT gains are larger at layer11.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of SAE disentanglement on cross-seed alignment depends on architecture and depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Source SAE latents improve ridge prediction of NSD higher ventral stream voxels: +13.9% for ResNet50 and +3.5% for ViT-B/16 (subject 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents of vision DNNs can improve linear predictivity of human ventral visual cortex.

record.problems: For real DNNs, the authors say they cannot directly verify the feature superposition arrangements; SAE-created representations or other factors could explain alignment increases. They report limited DNN-to-DNN and DNN-to-brain results, note known SAE limitations, and present several alignment values only in figures. Brain-alignment results in the main text give percentages for one representative subject; remaining subjects are described as consistent with results shown in an appendix figure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Regression comparisons for toy models and DNN-to-DNN results in Figure 4 are not separately cataloged because the text gives only broad qualitative summaries and the figures provide the values; the extracted rows prioritize the explicitly described soft-matching outcomes and the text-stated brain-prediction improvements.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B neuron audit or job shares.
All: no language models are studied; only toy models, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16.
All: the cat-and-car neuron is mentioned only as a background example of polysemanticity; it is not re-examined.
All: no interpretable-neuron shares, and no comparison of tools or architectures for neuron interpretability.
All: no attribution graphs or circuits.
All: no neuron explanations are tested against where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's framing assumes that polysemantic neurons reflect superposition. Its introduction cites a cat-and-car neuron as an example. That stance is the opposite of V3 and V4, but the paper gives no evidence on neuron interpretability itself, so no verdicts are given. The relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'assumes' because superposition is the paper's premise rather than a topic it argues about. Figure 4 regression results and the Appendix A.4 semi-matching results are not rows, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and shares of poles with one job, two jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Interpretability shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization.
The proposed causes of messy neurons and the estimated change in interpretable share for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs and whether they explain model behavior without a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
